final_answer:
The origin is uniformly globally exponentially stable under arbitrary switching exactly when

\[
\boxed{ab<4.}
\]

Let

\[
N_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&a\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
N_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\b&0\end{pmatrix},
\]

so \(A_i=-I+N_i\). Put \(x(t)=e^t z(t)\). Then

\[
\dot x(t)=N_{\sigma(t)}x(t).
\]

Now rescale coordinates. Let \(p=\sqrt{ab}\) and take \(D=\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt b,\sqrt a)\). For \(y=Dx\),

\[
\dot y(t)=pB_{\sigma(t)}y(t),
\]

where

\[
B_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
B_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]

For either mode,

\[
\frac{d}{dt}\|y\|^2
=2p\,y_1y_2
\le p(y_1^2+y_2^2)
=p\|y\|^2.
\]

Hence

\[
\|y(t)\|\le e^{pt/2}\|y(0)\|.
\]

Returning to \(z\),

\[
\|z(t)\|
\le \|D^{-1}\|\|D\|\,e^{-(1-p/2)t}\|z(0)\|.
\]

Thus if \(p<2\), i.e. \(ab<4\), the system is uniformly globally exponentially stable.

It remains to show this condition is sharp. Consider periodic switching with equal small dwell time \(\varepsilon\). For the \(y\)-system, one period gives

\[
e^{p\varepsilon B_1}e^{p\varepsilon B_2}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
1+p^2\varepsilon^2&p\varepsilon\\
p\varepsilon&1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Its spectral radius satisfies

\[
\frac{1}{2\varepsilon}\log\rho\!\left(e^{p\varepsilon B_1}e^{p\varepsilon B_2}\right)
\to \frac p2
\qquad(\varepsilon\to0).
\]

For the original \(z\)-system, the exponential factor \(-I\) subtracts \(1\), so the achievable growth rate tends to

\[
\frac p2-1.
\]

If \(p>2\), this gives exponential growth for some switching signal, so stability fails. If \(p=2\), the decay rates can be made arbitrarily close to \(0\), so no uniform exponential rate \(\gamma>0\) can hold.

Therefore the required set is

\[
\boxed{\{(a,b):a>0,\ b>0,\ ab<4\}}.
\]
